steps.label: Do Now: Order Matters
steps.content:
Do Now: Order Matters

No code yet. This is about the everyday idea we will build the whole lesson on: instructions only make sense in the right order.

items.prompt: You are making a cup of tea. Which order of steps makes sense?
options: Boil the kettle, then put a teabag in the cup, then pour the water in
Pour the water in, then boil the kettle, then put a teabag in the cup
Put a teabag in the cup, then pour the water in, then boil the kettle
items.explain: Each step depends on the one before it being finished - you cannot pour boiling water before the kettle has boiled it.

items.prompt: A recipe lists its steps in a specific order. If you swapped two of the steps around, what would you expect?
options: The result could come out wrong, because some steps rely on earlier steps already being done
The recipe would run twice as fast
items.explain: A sequence only works if every step assumes the ones before it have already happened - this is exactly what a computer program needs too.

steps.label: Sequence and Trace Tables
steps.content:
Algorithms

Sequence and Trace Tables

Year 11, Unit 7 L1

  • Explain what a sequence is, in plain English, before seeing any code.
  • Understand what a variable stores and what the arrow <- means.
  • Follow simple programs one line at a time, checking your answer at every step.
  • Build up to writing a short sequence yourself, one line at a time.

steps.label: What Is a Variable?
steps.content:
What Is a Variable?

Before we look at any code, let's get this one idea completely clear.

A variable is like a labelled box that stores one value at a time.

  • The label is the variable's name - for example, a box labelled Score.
  • The box can only ever hold one value at a time.
  • Putting a new value into the box removes whatever was in it before - the old value is gone.

Example

A box labelled Score holds 5. Later, the value 8 is put into that same box.

The box now holds 8. The 5 is not stored anywhere any more - it has been replaced.

steps.label: Check: What's in the Box?
steps.content: Check: What's in the Box?

items.prompt: A box labelled Age holds 12. Later, the value 15 is put into the same box. What does the box hold once both of these have happened?
items.explain: Putting a new value into a variable always replaces the old one - a variable never holds more than one value at a time.

items.prompt: A box labelled Colour holds "Red". Nothing else happens to it for the rest of the program. What does it hold at the end?
options: It depends on what other variables hold
items.explain: A variable keeps its value until something specifically changes it. Nothing changed Colour, so it still holds "Red".

steps.label: The Assignment Arrow: <-
steps.content:
The Assignment Arrow: <-

In pseudocode, "put this value in the box" is written using an arrow.

Score <- 5

This line means: put 5 into the box called Score.

It is an instruction, not a maths statement - it does not mean "Score equals 5" the way an equals sign does in maths. It means "store this value here, right now".

steps.label: Check: One Line of Code
steps.content: Check: One Line of Code

items.prompt: This single line runs: Score <- 5. What does Score contain afterwards?
items.explain: The arrow means "store this value in the box" - so Score now holds 5.

items.prompt: This single line runs: Age <- 10. What does Age contain afterwards?
items.explain: Same idea, different variable name - Age now holds 10.

steps.label: Instructions Run in Order, Top to Bottom
steps.content:
Instructions Run in Order, Top to Bottom

A sequence is a list of instructions that run one at a time, always starting at the top - exactly like the tea example earlier.

  • The computer finishes the first instruction completely before starting the second.
  • If an instruction uses a variable, it always uses whatever value is currently stored in the box - never a value from earlier or later.
  • To work out a new value: work out the right-hand side of the arrow first, using the current values, then store the result in the box on the left.

steps.content:
Follow a Program Line by Line

Watch how the value stored in Score changes, one line at a time.

steps.label: Checked Practice: One Variable
steps.content:
Checked Practice: One Variable

Work through this program the same way as the last one. Fill in the value stored in Number after each line runs.

1  Number <- 6
2  Number <- Number + 4
3  Number <- Number * 2
4  OUTPUT Number
Total: 4 marks

steps.label: Trace a Sequence
steps.content:
Trace a Sequence

Open Trace Tables and use the Sequence walkthrough. The algorithm starts with the input 4, then changes the value twice before producing an output.

Instructions

  1. Stay on the Walkthrough tab and select Sequence.
  2. Predict the final output before pressing Step Forward.
  3. Press Step Forward once for each executed line.
  4. Notice that a new row only appears when the variable changes or an output occurs.

Complete the walkthrough, then return to this lesson.

steps.label: Follow Two Variables
steps.content:
Follow Two Variables

  • Each variable has its own current value, tracked separately.
  • An instruction may use the current value of a different variable.
  • A later instruction always uses the newest stored value.
  • Output displays a value without changing what is stored.

steps.label: Checked Practice: Two Variables
steps.content:
Checked Practice: Two Variables

This program uses two boxes, First and Second. Track them separately.

1  First <- 8
2  Second <- 3
3  First <- First + Second
4  Second <- First * 2
5  OUTPUT First
6  OUTPUT Second
Total: 4 marks

steps.label: Complete a Sequence Trace Table
steps.content:
Complete a Sequence Trace Table

Open Trace Tables, choose the Practice tab and select Sequence. This algorithm uses a different input and different calculations from the walkthrough.

How to complete the table

  1. Read the input shown above the code.
  2. Start at line 1 and follow the code from top to bottom.
  3. Enter a value only when the variable changes or output occurs.
  4. Leave the other cells blank.
  5. Select Check Answers and correct every highlighted cell.

Complete Sequence Foundations successfully, then return to the lesson.

steps.label: Build a Sequence, One Line at a Time
steps.content:
Build a Sequence, One Line at a Time

Here is a complete seven-line program, except for four blanks. Most of the program is already written for you - just work out what each blank must be, using what you already know about the arrow and about following instructions in order.

1  INPUT A
2  INPUT B
3  Total <- (a)
4  Total <- Total * 2
5  Result <- (b)
6  OUTPUT (c)
7  OUTPUT (d)

INPUT A means: ask the user to type a value and store it in A. Lines 1 and 2 are already given as an example of this.

Total: 6 marks

steps.label: Sequence Exam Practice
steps.content:
Sequence Exam Practice

A real exam-style question. Follow the program exactly as written, using the newest value stored in each variable.

1  Value <- 7
2  Value <- Value - 2
3  Value <- Value * 3
4  OUTPUT Value
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Sequence Exam Practice, Part 2
steps.content:
Sequence Exam Practice, Part 2

One more real exam-style question, this time with two variables.

1  A <- 4
2  B <- 3
3  A <- A + B
4  B <- A * 2
5  OUTPUT A
6  OUTPUT B
Total: 4 marks

y11l1_practice_1.feedback: OUTPUT displays the current value, 20, without changing it.

y11l1_formative.feedback: Total needs to store A plus B, so the arrow is followed by A + B.
Result needs to store Total minus B, so the arrow is followed by Total - B.
Line 6 outputs the value stored in Total.
Line 7 outputs the value stored in Result.
